summary: This work introduces crosstalk-robust gate sets (CRGS) designed via optimal control to suppress pairwise quantum crosstalk in parallel single-qubit operations on superconducting qubit devices. Demonstrations on IBM Brisbane (127-qubit Eagle processor with heavy-hex layout) and in-house transmon hardware show $4\times$ median improvement in transverse-field Ising model simulation fidelity, $4$–$5\times$ reduction in decay rates under dynamical decoupling, and enable faster two-qubit gates through hardware–software co-design.
motivation: Quantum crosstalk from always-on static couplings between transmons degrades fidelity in multi-qubit circuits and limits scalability; software-only approaches avoid hardware overhead but have not been comprehensively evaluated at the algorithmic level.
method: Optimal control problems minimizing error susceptibility $\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{Z}; H_{\text{error}})$ to $ZZ$ crosstalk are formulated using graph coloring of the device connectivity. The approach achieves linear scaling by exploiting locality: the total crosstalk sensitivity factors as $\sum_{i,j \in E} \bar{\mathcal{R}}(\mathbf{Z}_i, \mathbf{Z}_j, \sigma_Z^{(i)}\sigma_Z^{(j)})$, requiring only independent two-qubit trajectories. CRGS are calibrated using standard Qiskit Pulse routines and integrated via a transpilation pass that schedules parallel gates without crosstalk accumulation.
result: On IBM Brisbane: random Clifford circuits show $1.6\%$ simultaneous four-qubit gate error versus $9.3\%$ for Gaussian gates; $XY_4$ dynamical decoupling achieves $0.039$ MHz decay rate over $0.163$ MHz for baseline on eight qubits. TFIM simulation reaches $50\times$ better accuracy after one Trotter step and $4\times$ median improvement. Simulations predict $3.4\times$ and $11.3\times$ fidelity improvements over detuning-robust and Gaussian gates at $J=2$ coupling, with two-qubit gate times reduced by half while maintaining performance.
